abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Silver nanoparticles against antimicrobial-resistant pathogens: in vivo efficacy, toxicokinetics, and barriers to clinical translation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is responsible for an estimated 1.27 million deaths annually, driving urgent demand for novel therapeutics. Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) have attracted significant interest due to their multi-target antibacterial activity, which presents a higher evolutionary barrier to resistance compared to conventional single-target antibiotics. However, AgNP monotherapy is limited by a narrow, formulation-dependent systemic therapeutic window, whereas repeated sublethal exposure may promote adaptive phenotypes. Combination with conventional antibiotics may enhance antimicrobial activity while reducing the concentrations of individual agents. This review examines theevidence for the efficacy of AgNPs against resistant pathogens, the physicochemical determinants governing their biological activity, and the translational barriers that limit clinical application. Whileliterature provides preclinical evidence of antibacterial efficacy and potential synergistic activity of AgNP-antibiotic combinations, systemic infections caused by priority pathogens remain understudied. Consequently, four critical translational gaps are identified: 1) the absence of a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) dosing framework; 2) insufficient systemic infection models; 3) limited understanding of potential effects on polymicrobial communities; and 4) inconsistent physicochemical characterization limiting cross-study comparison. Addressing these gaps through integrated preclinical evaluation will be essential for determining whether AgNPs can serve as safe and effective adjuvants to existing antimicrobial therapies.

title: Maternal and Neonatal Group B Streptococcus in Brazil: A Systematic Review Highlighting Epidemiological Gaps and Opportunities for Improved Prevention
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a major cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality worldwide. In Brazil, national data on GBS epidemiology remain scarce. We aimed to provide a comprehensive synthesis of maternal carriage, neonatal disease, serotype distribution, and antimicrobial resistance. We did a systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42023427476) following PRISMA 2020. PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, LILACS/SCIELO, and CINAHL were searched for studies published between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2024. Meta-analyses were performed using StataNow/SE version 19.5 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Pooled prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the metaprop command and random-effects models, and between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Forest plots were generated to illustrate pooled estimates. Forty-nine studies were included. Forty-three studies (n=64,658 samples) reported maternal GBS carriage, with a pooled prevalence of 17% (95% CI 14-20%; I=98.55%). Eight studies, encompassing more than 32 million live births, assessed early-onset neonatal disease, and reported incidence estimates of 0.01-0.45 per 1,000 live births. Among 1,502 maternal and neonatal isolates, serotypes Ia, V, II and III predominated, in descending order of prevalence. Among 9,880 maternal isolates, pooled resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin was 12% and 14%, respectively; penicillin non-susceptibility was rare. GBS burden in Brazil is substantial but poorly defined. Strengthening laboratory diagnosis of invasive neonatal GBS disease, implementing accessible capsular serotyping methods, and expanding geographically representative surveillance are priorities to improve disease burden estimates and inform prevention policies, including future maternal GBS vaccine implementation.

title: Integrating Pan-Genomics and Machine Learning into Foodborne Pathogen Traceability
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has become central to the investigation of foodborne outbreaks and the surveillance of bacterial pathogens, including Salmonella enterica, Listeria monocytogenes, Campylobacter spp., and Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli. Routine workflows rely heavily on core-genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) and reference-based single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis. These approaches provide reproducible measures of relatedness but do not systematically represent plasmids, prophages, genomic islands, and other accessory elements that can influence antimicrobial resistance (AMR), virulence, host adaptation, and persistence. Pan-genome analysis offers a way to examine both core and accessory variation, while machine learning (ML) can use these genomic features to estimate source, phenotype, and risk. This narrative review evaluates how these approaches are being integrated into foodborne pathogen traceability. We describe the strengths and limitations of core-genome typing, review genomic feature representations and learning algorithms, and assess applications in host and geographic attribution, virulence assessment, and AMR prediction. Particular attention is given to study design, including population-structure-aware data splitting, fold-specific preprocessing, external validation, and comparisons of core-only, accessory-only, and combined feature sets. The evidence supports a complementary, dual-pathway framework rather than replacement of established typing methods: cgMLST and SNP analysis remain well suited to rapid, auditable cluster detection, whereas pan-genome-informed ML can add probabilistic predictions of biological function and risk. Progress toward routine use will depend on representative benchmarks, transparent reporting, biological interpretation, and validation in operational settings.

title: Expanded granular sludge blanket coupled aerobic membrane bioreactor treating swine wastewater: Simultaneous removal of organics-ciprofloxacin and distribution of antibiotic resistance genes
abstract: As a class of emerging contaminants, antibiotics in swine wastewater at trace level pose potential ecological and environmental risks. The inhibition of biological treatment systems and the proliferation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have raised a widespread public attention. In this study, a coupled expanded granular sludge blanket (EGSB)-aerobic membrane bioreactor (AeMBR) was operated for 210 days to treat synthetic swine wastewater containing 150 ± 10 μg/L ciprofloxacin (CIP). The results demonstrated that the EGSB-AeMBR system achieved removal efficiencies of 98.4 ± 0.8% for COD, 68.5 ± 7.2% for CIP, and 90.3 ± 17.0% for NH-N. The relative abundance of the dominant Firmicutes in the anaerobic granular sludge decreased over the operational period, whereas Desulfobacterota and Synergistota increased, indicating microbial community succession under sustained CIP exposure. Metagenomic analysis revealed that the abundance of ARGs in the sludge from each unit exhibited a temporal succession pattern of an initial increase followed by a decrease. Real-time PCR results showed that the EGSB-AeMBR system effectively reduced ARGs in the liquid, with a logarithmic removal rate ranging from 2.75 to 5.08 log. However, the continuous accumulation of ARGs in the sludge may become a secondary pollution source. These findings provide long-term experimental evidence for pollutants simultaneous removal and unit-specific ARGs fate in a coupled high-rate treatment system.

title: Population-scale identification of gut commensals that antagonize antibiotic-resistant pathogens
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a global threat, yet microbiome-encoded defenses against antibiotic resistance gene (ARG)-associated pathogens remain poorly defined. Here, we analyze 12,238 human gut metagenomes and prioritize 159 commensal species ("coexcluders") that show inverse associations with ARG-associated pathogenic taxa. These taxa carry low ARG burdens and encode candidate antimicrobial peptide repertoires. For Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, deep learning-guided mining of 2,053 genomes reveals 6,737 peptides prevalent in the human gut that inversely associate with ARG-associated pathogens. In antibiotic-perturbed mice, F. prausnitzii reduces the resistance burden and restores ecological stability, with peptide enrichment. These peptides show preferential activity against antibiotic-resistant E. coli derivatives while sparing commensals, which is consistent with a kill-the-winner dynamic. Anaerobic coculture reveals resistance-dependent peptide induction, linking the resistance phenotype to competitive suppression. This work establishes a scalable, resistance-guided framework that links population-level ecological signatures to strain-resolved microbial and molecular candidates, providing a basis for mechanistic and therapeutic development.

title: Evaluating the antibiofilm effect of EPS-ZnO nanoparticles against Staphylococcus aureus biofilm and analysing its cytotoxic potential
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in foodborne pathogens like methylene-resistant(MRSA) requires sustainable alternatives. This study evaluates the multifunctional efficacy of green-synthesized, exopolysaccharide-mediated zinc oxide nanoparticles. EPS-ZnONP exhibited potent antibiofilm activity against S. aureus (MIC at 6 µg/ml; 20 mm inhibition zone at 10 µg/ml). SEM and fluorescence analysis elucidated strong antibiofilm potential revealing dense staphylococcal cell clusters in untreated samples while the treated samples showed biofilm eradication and cell shrinkage. Quorum sensing-associated virulence was markedly attenuated, showing a 24.9 ± 3.99% reduction in cell surface hydrophobicity at 100 μg/mL and strong inhibition of staphyloxanthin production. In Vigna radiata sprouts, EPS-ZnONPs boosted secondary metabolites and antioxidant capacity, peaking at 60 ppm with elevated total phenolics (2.27 ± 0.005 mg GAE/g), total flavonoids (7.46 ± 0.02 mg QE/g), saponins (0.486 mg/g), and DPPH radical scavenging (32.59 ± 0.04%). Primary metabolic reserves peaked distinctively, with carbohydrates reaching 128.6 ± 0.05 mg/g at 40 ppm and proteins hitting 0.79 ± 0.002 mg/g at 60 ppm. Biosafety assessments in zebrafish (Danio rerio) demonstrated enhanced growth kinetics and survival rates, alongside intact genomic DNA and RNA profiles confirming zero genotoxicity. Cytocompatibility was verified via MTT assay, retaining 92.7% viability in V79 fibroblasts (100 μg/mL) and 76.2% in A375 melanoma cells (50 μg/mL). These statistically significant (p < 0.05) outcomes validate EPS-ZnONPs as secure, multifunctional agents for biomedical and agricultural applications.

title: Global advances in laboratory medicine: the role of research funding in driving innovation and clinical translation
abstract: Laboratory medicine is undergoing rapid transformation as global health systems face population aging, chronic disease expansion, emerging infections, antimicrobial resistance, cancer survivorship, and increasing demand for precision diagnostics. Advanced diagnostic technologies are reshaping the field by enabling ultrasensitive biomarker detection, multiplexed molecular analysis, high-throughput testing, real-time monitoring, point-of-care diagnostics, laboratory automation, and data-supported interpretation. However, the clinical translation of these technologies depends not only on scientific progress, but also on the structure, continuity, and strategic orientation of research funding. This review summarizes the global development of advanced laboratory medicine technologies and highlights the role of public funding systems in shaping their scientific direction and translational trajectory. The comparative analysis of National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), National Institutes of Health (NIH), European Research Council (ERC), and United Kingdom Research and Innovation (UKRI) shows that funding systems are not passive sources of financial support. Rather, they influence which scientific questions are pursued, which technology platforms are prioritized, which teams are assembled, and how far discoveries can progress toward clinical implementation. Overall, effective funding systems do more than sponsor research; they actively shape how laboratory medicine evolves from scientific innovation toward validated, scalable, and clinically meaningful diagnostic practice.

title: Protocol to infect human airway air-liquid interface cultures with Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a WHO priority pathogen causing severe airway infections. Studying P. aeruginosa infections in human airways is crucial to understand treatment efficacy, antimicrobial resistance, and infection dynamics. We present a protocol to establish and infect airway air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures with P. aeruginosa. We describe human airway epithelial and P. aeruginosa culture techniques and how to perform infections of ALI cultures. We further describe downstream assays to assess infection, including barrier integrity, bacterial burden quantification, and infection visualization. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Colque et al..

title: Disruption of Staphylococcus aureus biofilm architecture by Myrica esculenta bark extract: in vitro and in silico perspectives
abstract: is a notorious pathogen distinguished by its robust capacity to form biofilms, a key factor for host immune evasion and antibiotic resistance. In the quest for novel antibiofilm agents, revisiting traditional medicinal knowledge - particularly plant-based therapies - offers a promising strategy., an ethnomedicinal Himalayan plant, is widely used in folk medicine for treating respiratory, gastrointestinal disorders, wound care, and toothache. Although preliminary studies on the antibacterial activity of its bark extract againsthave been reported, its antibiofilm potential remains unexplored. In this study, six solvents were systematically evaluated for extraction efficiency frombark, with methanol yielding the highest metabolite recovery (33.79%) and exhibiting strong antibacterial activity with MIC of 1 mg/mL. The extract significantly inhibited biofilm initiation and disrupted mature biofilms of(Newman) in a dose-dependent manner (MIC to 4 × MIC), accompanied by reduced exopolysaccharide production and decreased surface colonization. GC-MS analysis identified eight bioactive compounds, while molecular docking with the aggregation-prone region of the biofilm-associated protein (Bap) revealed strong binding affinities for key constituents. Additionally, membrane damage and bactericidal effects were confirmed. Toxicity assessment revealed no toxicity to HEK-293 mammalian cells, highlighting its safe therapeutic potential.

title: A novel gut microbiome-derived Tenebrionidae bacteriophage for biocontrol of Salmonella Typhimurium: in vitro characterization and in vivo evaluation in zebrafish
abstract: The global rise in antibiotic resistance has heightened interest in alternative biocontrol strategies, including bacteriophages and their endolysins. In this study, a new lytic bacteriophage, VB-STMS-SemU (hereafter SemU), was isolated from the gut microbiome of Opatroides punctulatus. It was purified using Salmonella Typhimurium as a host. Results showed that SemU exhibits siphovirus-like morphology, with an icosahedral capsid and a long, non-contractile tail. The host range includes Salmonella Typhimurium, Salmonella Enteritidis, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Kinetic analysis indicated an MOI of 1, an adsorption time of 17 min, a latent period of 70 min, and a burst size of 192 virions per cell. The phage-derived protein extract degraded 17% of the cell wall and was more effective than the whole phage at eradicating biofilms. No cytotoxicity was observed in eukaryotic cells. In zebrafish, about 10% of the phage was absorbed within 3 h, and no neutralizing antibodies were detected. Although an initial MOI of 1 was insufficient due to physiological barriers, increasing it to 10 significantly decreased intestinal bacterial loads. Phage titers peaked on day 3 and dropped to undetectable levels by day 7. SemU is a promising candidate for treating enteric infections.

title: Occurrence, distribution, and risk assessment of antibiotic residues in surface water, sediments, and drinking water from the Dunga wetland, Kisumu, Kenya
abstract: The contamination of water resources by antibiotic residues poses serious public health risks and significant environmental challenges owing to their adverse effects on the ecosystem and human health. However, information on their occurrence, distribution, and risks in Kenyan wetlands and drinking water remains scarce. This study reports the presence and potential risks of selected antibiotics in the Dunga wetland along Lake Victoria, which receives effluents from the Kisumu city wastewater lagoons. Sediment and water samples were collected from the upper, middle, and lower sections of the wetland and analyzed for six commonly used antibiotics: amoxicillin trihydrate, ciprofloxacin, flucloxacillin, sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim, and levofloxacin. We sampled drinking water before and after treatment at the Dunga drinking water treatment facility. The selected antibiotics were extracted from the water and sediment samples using solid-phase extraction. Instrumental analysis was done using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. All six antibiotics were detected across water and sediment matrices within the wetland. Compared with surface water samples, sediment samples contained more detectable antibiotic residues and had higher concentrations. Ciprofloxacin and sulfamethoxazole were the most prevalent antibiotics, with maximum concentrations of 3.4 ngL⁻in water and 3.7 ngkg⁻in sediment. The Dunga drinking water treatment facility achieved removal efficiencies of 95% for amoxicillin trihydrate and 6.4% for ciprofloxacin. Human health quotient values were several orders of magnitude below one, confirming no non-carcinogenic risk under current exposure conditions. The ciprofloxacin concentrations exceeded the minimum selective concentration threshold for antimicrobial resistance, suggesting potential long-term ecological disruptions and public health risks. The residual concentrations observed in this study demonstrate that conventional water treatment systems are inadequate for the effective removal of certain antibiotics from water. These findings help bridge the knowledge gap on the occurrence of antibiotics in wetland systems within developing countries and their associated risks. The adoption of enhanced wetland technologies within the Dunga Wetland ecosystem is recommended to improve the removal efficiency of antibiotic residues and other contaminants.

title: Advances in metal-organic frameworks for antibiotic removal from water: mechanisms, performance, challenges, and sustainable applications
abstract: Antibiotics are commonly found in water, posing risks to ecosystems and potentially contributing to the spread of antimicrobial resistance. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have attracted attention because their structures, surface properties, and active sites can be designed for antibiotic removal. This review critically examines MOFs for removal of antibiotic pollutants from water, focusing on the relationships among material properties, removal mechanisms, treatment performance, and practical application. The review compares adsorption and degradation by examining their mechanisms, removal performance, advantages, and limitations. It also investigates degradation pathways, transformation products, mineralization, and changes in toxicity to assess treatment-related environmental risks. The review also highlights key challenges to practical use, including stability, metal leaching, regeneration, treatment costs, and limited evaluation in real wastewater. Based on these findings, future research should concentrate on improving material stability, assessing the toxicity of degradation by-products, preventing secondary pollution, and testing MOFs in real wastewater. Future research should focus on improving material stability, assessing the toxicity of degradation by-products, preventing secondary pollution, and testing MOFs in real wastewater. By linking material properties and removal mechanisms to treatment performance and environmental safety, this work identifies key research directions for developing effective, sustainable MOF-based materials for antibiotic removal from wastewater.

title: Evolution of Chromosomal and Plasmid-Encoded β-Lactamases in Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter and Shared Features of VIM with NDM and IMP
abstract: β-lactamases (BLs) are primary drivers of antibiotic resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii, Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This study presents the first integrated evolutionary analysis of chromosomal AmpC β-lactamases (ADC, ACT, PDC) and plasmid-encoded metallo-β-lactamases or MBLs (NDM, VIM, IMP) across these three priority pathogens. Protein-protein interaction analysis identified NagZ as the central BL-interacting partner across Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, highlighting its potential as a drug target. Patristic distance analysis revealed progressive erosion of phylogenetic signal among MBLs, with NDM retaining the strongest structure, VIM intermediate, and IMP the least, while chromosomally encoded proteins consistently showed a conserved inter-organism proximity pattern. Discrete trait migration analysis revealed that inter-host gene flow of MBLs is greatest between phylogenetically distant lineages, suggesting selection-driven rather than neutral dissemination. GC content analysis confirmed NDM as the most globally sequence-conserved MBL and IMP the least. When protein features were used as descriptors for clustering, VIM clustered between IMP and NDM. Thus, multiple analyses showed that VIM exhibits intermediate characteristics between IMP and NDM. PFAM analysis also demonstrated that VIM shares domains from both NDM and IMP. Motif analysis identified a universally conserved FYPG(P/A)(G/A)H(T/S) element across all MBL families studied and the PGFGAVASNGLI motif showing cross-family similarity across all three MBLs. FADE functional divergence analysis revealed that sites surrounding the active site rather than active site itself are under high mutational pressure. These findings provide actionable insights into conserved sequence elements and evolutionary dynamics for broad-spectrum BL inhibitor design.

title: Antimicrobial activity of honeybee-gut-derived isolate E5 against multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa: molecular detection and expression analysis of mexA, mexB, and oprM
abstract: Multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa represents an important antimicrobial-resistance concern, highlighting the need to investigate alternative sources of antimicrobial activity. This study evaluated the in vitro antimicrobial activity of a cell-free supernatant (CFS) derived from Enterococcus faecium against clinical P. aeruginosa isolates and investigated selected efflux-associated gene expression responses. A total of 67 confirmed P. aeruginosa isolates were evaluated for antimicrobial susceptibility using the specified antimicrobial susceptibility testing procedure. The E. faecium-derived CFS was prepared by removing bacterial cells from the culture, and its antimicrobial activity was assessed using the agar well-diffusion method and minimum inhibitory dilution analysis. Selected culture conditions were evaluated to determine their effects on CFS antimicrobial activity. Nine representative P. aeruginosa isolates were selected for molecular analyses, while RT-qPCR analysis of mexA, mexB, and oprM expression was performed in two selected isolates, Z4 and 73. Gene-expression data were normalized using the selected reference gene and analyzed using the specified statistical procedures. Among the 67 P. aeruginosa isolates, antimicrobial susceptibility testing demonstrated substantial resistance to several tested antimicrobial agents, with the final resistance percentages reported consistently in Table 5 and the Results section. The E. faecium-derived CFS demonstrated measurable in vitro inhibitory activity against the tested P. aeruginosa isolates. The observed activity varied according to the tested culture conditions. The CFS also produced isolate-dependent changes in the transcription of mexA, mexB, and oprM in isolates Z4 and 73. In particular, the increased oprM expression observed in isolate 73 indicates that the transcriptional response was not uniform between isolates. The findings demonstrate in vitro antimicrobial activity of the E. faecium-derived CFS against P. aeruginosa under the conditions investigated. The RT-qPCR findings indicate isolate-specific changes in the transcription of selected efflux-associated genes. However, these transcriptional changes do not by themselves establish functional inhibition of the MexAB-OprM efflux pump or restoration of antimicrobial susceptibility. Because the CFS is a crude preparation and its active component(s) have not been definitively identified or purified, the findings should be considered preliminary and require further biochemical characterization, safety assessment, and functional and in vivo evaluation before any potential therapeutic application can be considered.

title: Targeting bacterial RNA repair: the Rtc system as an emerging antibiotic-adjuvant strategy
abstract: The RNA repair and rescue (Rtc) system is an emerging bacterial stress-response pathway that may support adaptation during antibiotic exposure. It comprises RNA 3'-phosphate cyclase RtcA, RNA ligase RtcB, and, in well-characterized models, the σ⁵⁴-dependent regulator RtcR. These components process and repair damaged RNA termini and may preserve translational capacity during ribotoxic, oxidative, and other stresses. Antibiotic-induced translational disruption can cause tRNA and rRNA cleavage or fragmentation, potentially increasing dependence on Rtc-mediated repair. Experimental evidence suggests that Rtc facilitates RNA recovery and bacterial survival during transient stress, although its importance varies among species and remains poorly defined under clinically relevant conditions. Rtc-mediated survival appears more closely associated with phenotypic stress tolerance than classical heritable antibiotic resistance, although prolonged survival may create opportunities for subsequent adaptation. Considerable diversity in Rtc organization, regulation, and physiological dependence also limits extrapolation from model bacteria to multidrug-resistant pathogens. The distinct catalytic and regulatory properties of RtcA, RtcB, and RtcR provide potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention. Proposed approaches include small-molecule inhibition, suppression of rtc expression, synthetic-lethal combinations, nanocarrier-mediated delivery, and engineered bacteriophages. However, no clinically validated Rtc-specific inhibitor is currently available, and these therapeutic applications remain largely conceptual or preclinical. Overall, the Rtc system represents an important area of bacterial RNA biology that warrants further investigation as a stress-associated vulnerability and potential target for future antibiotic-adjuvant strategies.

title: Clinical Utility of Nanopore-Based Targeted and Metagenomic Sequencing for Rapid Diagnosis of Infections
abstract: Rapid diagnosis is critical for acute invasive infections, yet conventional culture is time-consuming. The real-time, long-read capability of nanopore sequencing facilitates rapid diagnosis, but standardized workflows are lacking. Here, we describe 2 nanopore sequencing workflows, nanopore targeted sequencing (NTS) and nanopore metagenomic sequencing (NMgS), for pathogen and antimicrobial resistance identification. A total of 176 residual clinical specimens, of which >90% were abdominal, pleural, joint, abscess, and bile samples, were analyzed using the NTS and NMgS workflows and compared with culture. NTS employed multiplex PCR to amplify 16S rRNA gene, internal transcribed spacer region, and 30 resistance genes, while NMgS involved host DNA depletion and unbiased sequencing. Among 152 culture-positive samples, NTS achieved 98.68% positivity, compared with 69.08% for NMgS. NTS identified 79.93% of cultured species, while NMgS detected 44.89%. For 24 culture-negative samples, NTS identified potential pathogens in 6 cases, whereas NMgS detected none. For antimicrobial resistance detection, NTS achieved a sensitivity of 84.62% for β-lactam resistance, 62.50% for quinolones, and 31.25% for aminoglycosides, with corresponding specificities of 87.10%, 75.86%, and 96.61%. Conversely, NMgS showed lower sensitivities of 36.84%, 16.67%, and 12.50% for these classes, while maintaining 100% specificity across all categories. Using the 4-h sequencing workflow, NTS and NMgS achieved comparable sample-to-report times (10.83 vs 10.41 h). This study demonstrates the potential of nanopore sequencing for rapid diagnosis and provides practical insights for its implementation in clinical laboratories. While NTS is sensitive and cost-effective, NMgS offers a hypothesis-free approach. These workflows may complement routine culture in specific clinical contexts.

title: Salmonella enterica strains differ in the effect of AcrABZ-TolC mutation on cell motility and susceptibility to bacteriophage Chi
abstract: The rise in multidrug-resistant pathogenic bacteria has renewed interest in phage therapy. The lytic phage Chi is a broad host-range phage infecting,, and. Chi belongs to the group of flagellotropic phages, which require a rotating flagellum to infect host cells. We previously reported that mutations in genes encoding components of the AcrABZ-TolC efflux pump greatly reduce Chi infection ofTyphimurium strain 14028S (serotype Typhimurium [STM] 14028S). Here, we tested and rejected the hypothesis that the AcrABZ-TolC complex is the cell-surface receptor for Chi. First, STM 14028S mutants with an inactivating point mutation in the AcrB pump displayed decreased susceptibility to Chi. Second, STM 14028S mutants of individual AcrABZ-TolC components showed reduced motility on nutrient soft agar, and a ∆mutant exhibited an over 80% reduction in the number of motile cells. Together, these results suggest that Chi phage resistance may be mediated by an effect on motility rather than by loss of a cell surface receptor. Additionally, deletions of,, andin another Typhimurium strain, STM 4/74, and two other serotypes, Choleraesuis and Poona, retained susceptibility to Chi and had no apparent motility defects. Taken together, mutations in the AcrABZ-TolC pump caused reduced motility and, thereby, Chi infection in STM 14028S, but not in other tested strains. These results suggest that this pump is not a cell surface receptor for Chi. Phage therapy is of rising importance for combating antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Particularly, phages targeting structures important for virulence are of interest as they present an exploitable evolutionary tradeoff, as bacteria will likely lose virulence to become resistant to the phage. We previously reported that inTyphimurium strain 14028S, the AcrABZ-TolC efflux pump, an important virulence factor, was also required for infection by the flagellotropic phage Chi. We report here that this requirement for Chi infection is due to reduced motility of mutants, rather than AcrABZ-TolC being the cell-surface receptor. The reduction in motility caused by AcrABZ-TolC mutations in strain 14028S is not conserved across other strains andserotypes, including Poona and Choleraesuis.

title: Anoxia selects for high-fitness biofilms and reduces antibiotic susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a growing global health crisis, yet resistance is almost exclusively quantified under aerobic laboratory conditions that fail to reflect the complex microenvironments bacteria encounter during infection. Many clinically important infection sites, such as airways of individuals with cystic fibrosis or chronic wounds, are microaerobic to anoxic. To address this, we investigated how anoxia alters antibiotic resistance determinants, hypothesizing that anaerobic metabolism might change the fitness effects and selection of resistance mutations. We used experimental evolution to propagatepopulations for approximately 200 generations under conditions differing in oxygen availability (oxic vs anoxic), growth mode (biofilm vs planktonic), and tobramycin exposure (subinhibitory increasing to inhibitory concentrations). Subinhibitory exposure reduced susceptibility to tobramycin by 2×-4× compared to ancestral levels, with anoxic populations consistently having higher minimum inhibitory concentrations than oxic populations. Mutations inandarose across all conditions, but mutations inwere only selected in oxic populations-indicating condition-specific mutations in response to antibiotics. Notably,mutations were observed in anoxic or tobramycin-exposed populations. Anoxic populations exhibited significantly increased biofilm formation, reduced twitching motility driven by type IV pilus gene mutations, and greater competitive fitness. Together, these findings demonstrate that oxygen availability shapes the response to antibiotics in, with the anoxic environment selecting for reduced antibiotic susceptibility, higher fitness, and high biofilm-forming phenotypes. is an opportunistic pathogen capable of acute and chronic infections that develop antibiotic resistance. One aspect ofthat makes it so challenging to treat is its metabolic versatility. We wanted to understand how growth in different infection-relevant conditions, specifically anoxia and surface attachment, would alter the evolutionary pathways of antibiotic resistance. We found that the mutations causing reduced antibiotic susceptibility to the commonly used antibiotic tobramycin were condition dependent. We also observed that adaptation to anoxia resulted inpopulations that had high biofilm-forming capacity and were highly fit compared to their ancestors. This indicates that anoxic infection environments can lead tovariants with increased resistance, increased recalcitrance, and potentially more virulence.

title: Quantification of antimicrobials and surfactants in drain biofilms: rapid extraction and comprehensive LC-MS/MS analysis
abstract: Biofilms formed in drain environments may act as reservoirs of chemical residues that contribute to the development of antimicrobial resistance. The occurrence of surfactants and antimicrobials in such biofilms remains poorly understood, partly due to the lack of studies jointly quantifying these compound classes. In this study, we developed a simple and robust sample preparation workflow together with a quantitative LC-MS/MS method for simultaneous analysis of diverse antimicrobials and multiple classes of surfactants in drain biofilms. The method showed reliable overall analytical performance in validation biofilm samples, with no notable interference observed for most analytes. Compound-dependent absolute recoveries, covering analyte losses during sample processing and ion suppression or signal enhancement in the MS, ranged from 22 to 111%. However, spike recoveries of 72 to 103%, obtained after normalisation with internal standards, indicate reliable and accurate quantification even for the compounds with low absolute recoveries. Application of the method tobiofilm samples revealed high concentrations of surfactant compounds, highlighting the necessity of compound-specific dilution strategies and individual internal standards. Overall, the method simplifies sample preparation and enables rapid multi-class quantification of disinfectants, surfactants and antibiotics in complex biofilm matrices, enabling improved assessment of their role in biofilm-associated antimicrobial resistance.

title: The complete genome sequence of an Acinetobacter baumannii phage, Djidily-mokiny
abstract: can cause life-threatening infections in immunocompromised individuals. Here, a bacteriophage with activity againstisolated from wastewater was sequenced. It has a genome size of 80,562 bp and represents a potential new genus of bacteriophage. It has no genes associated with lysogeny, bacterial resistance, or virulence.

title: Antibiotic heteroresistance observed across commensal Lactobacillus species
abstract: Lactobacilli are prevalent members of the microbiota in the intestinal and reproductive tracts of humans and other species. They are commonly used in probiotics due to their beneficial effects on human health, including their association with protection from numerous chronic diseases. In addition, these microbes are often prescribed to maintain their presence in the host during antibiotic therapy, as well as to treat diarrhea caused by antibiotics. Despite many studies examining the beneficial effects of lactobacilli, less is known about how they survive during antibiotic treatment, and in particular, whether they exhibit heteroresistance, a phenotype in which only a minor subpopulation of resistant cells coexists with a majority susceptible population. Here, we tested representativespecies for heteroresistance to a broad panel of relevant antibiotics. The results demonstrate thatstrains, including those isolated from human feces, can exhibit heteroresistance to relevant antibiotics from distinct classes, and are often heteroresistant to fluoroquinolones. In particular, heteroresistance to fluoroquinolones was even observed inGG, a widely used probiotic. These findings significantly impact our understanding of how lactobacilli, including strains isolated from human samples, can survive antibiotic treatment, and how individual probiotic strains may be selected for use during antibiotic therapy to promote their survival and maximize their benefits. Commensal bacteria, such asspecies, are widely used for their beneficial effects on gastrointestinal health and their potential to help restore the gut microbial community after antibiotic use. However, the antibiotic resistance profiles of these beneficial bacteria have received limited attention despite their relevance to probiotic use. Heteroresistance is a phenomenon in which a small subpopulation of resistant bacteria within an otherwise susceptible community survives antibiotic exposure, but it is often undetected, underappreciated, and has largely not been investigated among commensal bacteria. Our study provides a characterization of heteroresistance across distinctspecies and a panel of antibiotics, revealing that heteroresistance is far more widespread than previously appreciated, especially to fluoroquinolones. These findings suggest probiotic strains could be selected that would survive concurrent antibiotic therapy and thus highlight that more comprehensive resistance profiling of probiotic bacteria may yield benefits to patients.

title: Multi-target anti-Salmonella activity of metabolites from Piper aduncum against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium: in vitro and in silico evidence
abstract: Salmonellosis is a major foodborne disease, and increasing antimicrobial resistance has intensified the search for new therapeutic agents. In this study, dillapiole and dihydroflavokawain B were isolated fromroots and evaluated for their anti-Salmonella activity againstserovar Typhimurium. Dihydroflavokawain B showed potent anti-activity (MIC = 12.1 µg/mL), while dillapiole exhibited moderate activity (MIC = 312.5 µg/mL). Molecular docking revealed favourable interactions with bacterial targets, especially for dihydroflavokawain B, which showed affinities comparable to reference antibiotics. In silico ADMET analyses indicated good oral bioavailability, intestinal absorption, and low predicted toxicity, highlightingas a promising source of anti-compounds.

title: Genomic characterization of Pediococcus acidilactici AB01 isolated from Algerian Targui camel milk: insights into safety, probiotic-associated traits, and functional potential
abstract: Pediococcus acidilactici displays substantial strain-level variation, requiring genome-resolved evaluation of new food-associated isolates. This study characterized P. acidilactici AB01, isolated from raw milk of Algerian Targui camels, and used previously generated in vitro observations only to contextualize genomic predictions. Illumina sequencing yielded a 2,117,438-bp draft genome with 42.0% GC content, 36 contigs, and an N50 of 389,234 bp. BUSCO recovered 99.2% complete markers, whereas CheckM estimated 98.23% completeness and 2.43% contamination. ANIb values calculated with IPGA were 99.01% and 98.71% relative to the P. acidilactici type-strain deposits DSM 20,284and JCM 8797, respectively; dDDH values of 91.2% supported species assignment. ResFinder detected no known acquired antimicrobial-resistance genes, and no virulence-factor match satisfied the predefined identity and reference-coverage criteria. CARD-RGI additionally identified three distant Strict homolog matches (sdrM-like, qacG-like, and alr/vanT-like), which were examined according to their sequence characteristics and genomic contexts. Functional annotation identified candidate genetic determinants potentially associated with stress responses, carbohydrate metabolism, and cell-surface interactions, together with a predicted Type II-A CRISPR-Cas locus containing 29 spacers with putative viral matches. Comparative analysis of 85 P. acidilactici genomes identified an open pan-genome comprising 5,485 clusters (Heaps-law γ = 0.266). Seventy-seven candidate clusters occurred only in AB01 within this dataset, of which 67 remained after excluding clusters containing partial coding-sequence annotations. Overall, these findings highlight the genomic diversity of P. acidilactici and identify AB01 as a promising candidate requiring further in-depth experimental evaluation before its safety and probiotic, biopreservative, or functional potential can be established.

title: Benzoxaboroles and Other Small Boron-Containing Organic Molecules of Biological Activity
abstract: The chapter focuses on organic boron derivatives, which means mainly benzoxaboroles and other organic single-boron containing biologically active compounds. Papers published over the last decade have been primarily covered to address recent developments in this area of research. Basic chemistry of boronic species has been presented to give the idea of unique properties of those derivatives, transferring to their medicinal applications as well as to give some hints for future development in this area. Structures of single boron containing drugs as well as compounds under clinical trials have been presented. The enormous importance of boron compounds in many branches of chemistry stems primarily from their potential for numerous interactions with various compounds found in living organisms. Benzoxaboroles and other small boron-containing compounds incorporate a C-B bond, which does not typically occur in nature. Its presence in the structure of potential drugs possibly alters the mechanism by which microorganisms develop resistance and gives hope for the development of novel potential drugs. This is particularly important given the growing problem of antibiotic resistance in microorganisms and the need to seek alternative therapies. Several small boron-containing molecules have already entered therapeutical use. Those cover two benzoxaboroles: antifungal tavaborole (Kerydin) and anti-inflammatory crisaborole (Eucrisa), a cyclic boronic hemiester; antibacterial vaborbactam (Vabomere); and two anticancer boronic acids - bortezomib (Velcade) and ixazomib (Ninlaro). Many other small boron-containing drugs are currently under development, and some of them reached clinical trials.

title: Antimicrobial non-susceptibility of presumptive commensal Escherichia coli in animals from farms and equestrian centres in Saint Petersburg and the Leningrad Region, Russia: prevalence and farm-level variation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in commensal bacteria from farm animals is an important One Health concern; however, data on antimicrobial susceptibility of commensal Escherichia coli in northwest Russia remain limited. A total of 158 non-duplicate presumptive E. coli isolates were obtained from faecal samples collected from horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and reindeer at 11 farms and equestrian centres in Saint Petersburg and the Leningrad Region. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined using the disk-diffusion method. Zone diameters for ampicillin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, cefotaxime, and meropenem were interpreted using the clinical breakpoints in CLSI M100 (34th edition), whereas furagin was interpreted using the disk manufacturer's criteria. All isolates were tested against ampicillin and ciprofloxacin; tetracycline and cefotaxime were tested in 86 isolates and furagin and meropenem in 72 isolates. For this study, non-susceptibility was defined as the combined intermediate and resistant categories (I + R). Among the 86 isolates tested for tetracycline and cefotaxime, 47 (54.7%) and 25 (29.1%) were classified as non-susceptible, respectively. Among the 158 isolates tested for ampicillin and ciprofloxacin, 58 (36.7%) and 44 (27.8%) were classified as non-susceptible, respectively. Of the 72 isolates tested for meropenem, 10 (13.9%) were classified as intermediate, and none as resistant. All 72 isolates tested against furagin were classified as susceptible according to the disk manufacturer's interpretive criteria. Marked variation in non-susceptibility was observed between farms. After accounting for clustering within farms, neither age nor sex was significantly associated with ampicillin or ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility. These findings provide baseline data for the sampled farms and equestrian facilities in Saint Petersburg and the Leningrad Region and underscore the value of farm-level surveillance of antimicrobial susceptibility in commensal E. coli.
