A multi-epitope vaccine based on AdeK, PirA, and Omp22 elicits specific antibodies binding to Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) as a critical-priority pathogen that requires novel antibiotics and strategies, due to its high antibiotic resistance. To combat the critical public health threat posed by CRAB, bioinformatics and immunoinformatic tools were used in this study to predict potential linear B lymphocyte (LBL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) epitopes derived from the Acinetobacter baumannii (A. baumannii) outer membrane proteins AdeK, PirA, and outer membrane protein 22 (Omp22). Subsequently, four combined multi-epitope vaccines (MEVs) designated ABV1-ABV4 were constructed by linking selected LBL, HTL, and CTL epitopes and Pan-HLA-DR reactive epitopes (PADRE) via GGGS and AAY linkers and fusing four different adjuvants to the N-terminus of the constructs with EAAAK linkers to increase immunogenicity. Afterward, the allergenicity, antigenicity, and solubility of ABV1-ABV4 were analyzed. The two non-allergenic candidates ABV3 and ABV4 were further analyzed for physicochemical properties and immune simulation using ExPASy ProtParam and C-ImmSim. ABV4 exhibited superior antigenicity and solubility compared with ABV3, and both ABV4 and ABV3 were predicted to induce similar immune responses; therefore, ABV4 was selected for further structural characterization and subsequent expression. The 3D structure was modeled using AlphaFold 3.0 and refined with GalaxyRefine servers. After refinement, the quality of the 3D structure improved markedly, with 97.2% of the residues in the most favored regions of the Ramachandran plot and an overall Z score of -6.11. Docking scores were -274.02 kcal/mol for ABV4-TLR2 and -302.54 kcal/mol for ABV4-TLR4. MM/PBSA calculations yielded binding free energies of -53.66 kcal/mol for ABV4-TLR2 and -68.93 kcal/mol for ABV4-TLR4. The optimized ABV4 gene was synthesized, cloned and inserted into pET28a, and expressed in E. coli BL21 with a C-terminal 6 × His tag. Immunization of mice with ABV4 induced high titers of anti-ABV4 antibodies and elevated serum IFN-γ and IL-4 levels, suggesting that ABV4 may elicit both humoral and cellular immune responses in mice. Immunofluorescence assay (IFA) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) revealed that the ABV4 antibody specifically recognized CRAB extracellular proteins without cross-reactivity to E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or P. aeruginosa, confirming that ABV4 is a promising MEV vaccine candidate against CRAB with the potential to induce humoral and cellular immune responses. Overall, ABV4 is a promising vaccine candidate against CRAB, and further experimental research is required to validate the protective efficacy in mice and elucidate the underlying mechanisms.

title: Determinants of antibiotic prescribing among physicians at tertiary teaching hospitals in Egypt: a cross-sectional study using the COM-B framework
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global health threat. Antibiotic prescribing is influenced by behavioural and system-level determinants beyond physicians’ knowledge. This study applies the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation–Behaviour (COM-B) framework to identify determinants influencing antibiotic prescribing and inform stewardship interventions. Cross-sectional analytical study. Tertiary teaching hospitals in Minia, Egypt, from October 2024 to May 2025. A total of 311 physicians were included in the study following stratified random sampling. The primary outcome was antibiotic prescribing practice, measured as a continuous composite prescribing-practice score. The secondary outcome was motivation towards antibiotic prescribing, classified using the motivation domain of the COM-B questionnaire. Associations with prescribing practice were examined using multivariable generalised linear regression, while factors associated with poor motivation were examined using multivariable binary logistic regression. Although physicians demonstrated good knowledge of AMR (87.5%), prescribing practice (39.6%) scores were suboptimal, revealing a knowledge–practice gap. Only 60.8% of physicians reported ordering antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and 24.9% did so consistently. More than half (59.2%) prescribed antibiotics against their preference, and 83.6% favoured brand-name prescribing. Perceived workload significantly affected practice; heavy (β=−10.21, p=0.001), overwhelming workload (β=−15.36, p<0.001) and managing 25–49 patients daily (β=−9.10, p=0.008) were associated with lower prescribing practice scores. Surgical specialty and older age were also associated with lower scores. Conversely, training attendance (β=7.67, p=0.016) and consultation time of 10–15 min (β=7.79, p=0.023) improved practice. Higher opportunity scores were significantly associated with reduced odds of poor motivation (OR=0.978, 95% CI 0.9to 0.99p<0.001). Despite relatively high knowledge level, lower practice level was observed among the participating physicians. Perceived workload, system constraints and behavioural factors may be relevant alongside knowledge in understanding prescribing practices. These findings highlight the relevance of a broader approach to antimicrobial stewardship that extends beyond knowledge-based education alone, with particular attention to structural opportunities, workload-related barriers and stewardship training.

title: Rural Environmental Improvement Reshapes the Airborne Microbiome and Reduces Pathogenic and Antibiotic Resistance Risks
abstract: Nationwide government-led Rural Environmental Improvement (REI) initiatives are being extensively implemented across China. However, it remains poorly understood how such improvements influence airborne microorganisms and the antibiotic resistome, both of which are closely linked to human health risks. Here, we employed a space-for-time substitution approach based on one-year continuous sampling, collecting 99 airborne samples from improved and unimproved villages for 16S rRNA amplicon and autumn-specific shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Our results indicated that REI restructured airborne microbial community composition, with greater impacts on abundant taxa than rare taxa. REI was further associated with reduced relative abundance of airborne potential pathogens, showing a tentative 14.0% reduction under good air quality conditions. Metagenomic analyses targeting autumn samples demonstrated a 34.6% decline in normalized ARG abundance. Furthermore, REI was associated with decreased mobility potential of ARGs and lower prevalence of ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs) carried by pathogenic bacteria. This study provides critical insights into how REI reshapes the atmospheric microbial communities and resistome profiles, highlighting its potential to mitigate atmospheric biological health risks. These findings provide microbial evidence to support health-oriented rural ecological management and sustainable development.

title: Extrapulmonary rapidly growing mycobacterial infections in Far North Queensland, tropical Australia, 2008-2024, a retrospective study
abstract: The global incidence of rapidly growing mycobacterial (RGM) infections is rising. We examined, retrospectively, cases of extrapulmonary RGM infection managed at a referral hospital in Far North Queensland (FNQ), tropical Australia, to characterise their presentation and the challenges in their management. All RGM isolated from extrapulmonary sites in FNQ residents between January 2008 and December 2024 were identified; the isolates' microbiological characteristics and the patients' clinical course were reviewed. Mycobacterium fortuitum group (59/144, 41%), Mycobacterium abscessus complex (46/144, 32%) and Mycobacterium chelonae (21/144, 15%) were the most frequently isolated RGM. Clinical infection was confirmed in 103/144 (72%) isolates. The annual incidence of RGM clinical infections increased over the study period from 0.4 to 2.4/100,000 population (r=0.57, p=0.02). Patients had a median (interquartile range (IQR)) age of 52 (33-66) years; 10/103 (10%) were immunosuppressed while only 6/103 (6%) had other significant comorbidity. Preceding environmental trauma was documented in 39/103 (38%), 38/103 (37%) followed surgery and 23/103 (22%) infections involved prosthetic material. The median (IQR) duration of symptoms at diagnosis was 5 (2-12) weeks. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing demonstrated high rates of resistance; 78 patients were treated with antibiotics for a median (IQR) duration of 18 (16-24) weeks with 47/78 (60%) experiencing an adverse drug reaction. Surgical management was necessary in 64/103 (62%). There were 6 microbiologically confirmed relapses but no deaths directly attributable to the infection or its treatment. Extrapulmonary RGM infections are increasing in frequency in tropical Australia and predominantly affect younger, healthy individuals. Delayed diagnosis and adverse events from antimicrobial therapy are common.

title: Fluvoxamine disrupts Enterococcus faecalis biofilms by downregulating adhesion genes and binding biofilm proteins: a promising strategy for antimicrobial urinary catheter coatings
abstract: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI) are predominantly driven by biofilm formation on indwelling devices, which significantly complicates treatment and contributes to high morbidity and mortality. The increasing antimicrobial resistance has intensified the need for novel therapeutic and preventive strategies. In this study, we investigated fluvoxamine, a selective serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, for its antibacterial and antibiofilm potential against Enterococcus faecalis, a common CAUTI pathogen. Fluvoxamine exhibited potent antibacterial activity with a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 12.5 µg/mL. Time-kill kinetics revealed rapid bactericidal activity within 1 h, and combination studies demonstrated synergistic effects with conventional antibiotics. Fluvoxamine significantly inhibited biofilm formation and eradicated up to 89% of preformed mature E. faecalis biofilms. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) corroborated these findings, revealing substantial disruption of biofilm architecture and morphological damage to bacterial cells. In ancatheter model, fluvoxamine-coated catheter tubes effectively reduced bacterial colonization and maintained antibacterial efficacy for up to 48 h. Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) combined with FDA/PI staining confirmed reduced biofilm thickness and increased proportion of dead cells. Molecular docking analysis indicated a strong binding affinity of fluvoxamine to keybiofilm-associated adhesion proteins. Furthermore, quantitative RT-PCR analysis showed significant downregulation of biofilm-related genes, including GelE, EbpA, AS, and EfaA. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that fluvoxamine possesses promising antibacterial and antibiofilm properties and highlight its potential as a novel catheter-coating agent for the prevention and management of-associated CAUTI.

title: Microplastics facilitate the enrichment of high-risk antibiotic resistance genes and pathogens in farming environments as mobile niches
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) represent a significant threat to human and animal health, as they function as concealed niches that can adsorb antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and pathogens. Although farming environments are recognized as significant sources of ARGs and pathogens, systematic research on the specific environmental risks associated with the co-exposure of MPs and these pollutants remains inadequate. In this study, we systematically investigated the selective enrichment of MPs as novel mobile niches for ARGs and related pathogens, as well as their roles in high-frequency exchange within livestock and poultry farming environments through in situ culture incubation experiments, metagenomic analyses, and the isolation and cultivation of drug-resistant strains. Our findings revealed that the abundance of ARGs on MPs was significantly higher than in the surrounding water bodies and sediments. The enriched genes included multidrug, bacitracin, and β-lactam resistance genes and high-risk resistance genes such as bla, bla, mcr, and tet(X). Additionally, mobile genetic elements (MGEs), metal resistance genes (MRGs), and virulence factors (VFs) were also significantly enriched on MPs. Notably, potential pathogens such as Acinetobacter, Aeromonas, and Pseudomonas exhibited selective enrichment on MPs. Host tracing analyses identified multiple bacterial hosts harboring ARGs, while source tracking and phylogenetic analyses of Escherichia coli demonstrated that the exchange of ARGs and pathogens can frequently take place between the livestock farming environment, primarily in sediments, and MPs. Overall, the results of this study provide important insights into assessing the potential risks posed by microplastics as mobile niches for the transmission of ARGs and pathogens in livestock and poultry farming environments.

title: Environmental fate of antibiotics, microplastics, and heavy metals under algal-bloom conditions: A review of interactions and ecological risks
abstract: The increasing co-occurrence of antibiotics, microplastics, and heavy metals in eutrophic waters has intensified concerns over combined pollution under algal-bloom conditions. This review synthesizes the formation mechanisms and environmental effects of algal blooms, the environmental behavior and monitoring approaches for these three pollutant classes, and the bidirectional interactions between algal blooms and such pollutants. Current evidence indicates that algal blooms can markedly alter pollutant speciation, partitioning, transport, and environmental fate through the secretion of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) secretion, cell-surface adsorption, heteroaggregation, buoyancy-driven transport, and bloom-induced changes in pH, dissolved oxygen, and redox conditions. In turn, antibiotics, microplastics, and heavy metals can regulate bloom initiation and decline by inducing oxidative stress and disrupting photosynthetic electron transport, and they drive the enrichment and dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in phycospheric microenvironments, the formation of an eco-corona on microplastic surfaces, and the transformation and re-release of heavy metals, collectively amplifying ecological risk and food-web transfer under combined-pollution scenarios. Overall, algal blooms are a likely consequence of eutrophication under suitable physical and biological conditions, and they can drive cross-media transport, interfacial redistribution, and the evolution of ecological risk for common pollutants. This review provides a framework for interpreting pollutant fate and ecological risk in aquatic systems affected by algal blooms and multiple contaminants.

title: Enhanced photodynamic performance of violet phosphorus nanosheets via covalent polyethylene-glycol modification for bacterial-infection therapy
abstract: Bacterial infections within the wound microenvironment and the exacerbation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) present significant challenges to skin tissue regeneration. Endowed with a "nano-knife" effect and photodynamic therapy (PDT) potential, violet phosphorus nanosheets (VPNS) have emerged as promising non-antibiotic antibacterial materials. However, their inherently poor colloidal stability severely limits their biomedical applications. To overcome this bottleneck, we functionalized VPNS with a diazonium-terminated polyethylene glycol (HO-PEG-AD)the formation of stable C-P covalent bonds, successfully constructing VPNS@PEG-AD nanocomposites. This modification significantly enhances the stable dispersion time in aqueous solutions and subsequently improves the efficiency of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation under light irradiation.assays demonstrated that VPNS@PEG-AD exhibits a potent synergistic antibacterial effect against bothandupon irradiation, driven by the dual action of physical piercing and ROS-mediated oxidative damage. Furthermore, in a murine model of-infected epidermal wounds, the VPNS@PEG-AD effectively eradicated infection, suppressed inflammatory cell infiltration, and significantly accelerated wound healing without exhibiting obvious systemic toxicity. In summary, this highly stable PEGylated VPNS nanoplatform provides a safe and highly efficient strategy for combating AMR and promoting the healing of infected wounds.

title: Assessment of the public health risk of fish offal: serotype diversity, virulence profiles, biofilm formation, and antibiotic resistance of Escherichia coli
abstract: Fish, while an important food source for human nutrition, can be contaminated with microorganisms for various reasons. Escherichia coli, a significant microorganism, is transmitted to humans through raw or undercooked meat, dairy products, and vegetables, potentially causing serious infections. Therefore, this study aimed to identify E. coli strains in fish carcasses and offal, analyze their virulence factors, diagnose their antibiotic resistance profiles, and determine their biofilm-formin e hundred fish samples were randomly selected from fish markets in Kayseri, Türkiye (August-December 2023). We serotyped the E. coli isolates obtained from these fish samples, tested them for antibiotic resistance (disk diffusion method), and determined their biofilm-forming capabilities. Furthermore, their gene profiles (virulence and antibiotic resistance genes) were determined using molecular techniques. Suspected E. coli isolates were identified using the trpA gene, and a total of 70 isolates (77%) were confirmed as positive. Additionally, E. coli serotypes O26 (7.1%), O111 (1.4%), O45 (1.4%), and H8 (11.4%) were identified. Antibiotic resistance rates were determined for ampicillin (17%), tetracycline (31%), erythromycin (41%), gentamicin (51%), and enrofloxacin (40%), and multidrug resistance was 37.1%. Virulence gene distributions in the isolates were determined using the stx2 (20%) and hlyA (1.4%) genes. E. coli virulence genes (stx1, eaeA, and hlyA) were tested. Although fish and offal provide an alternative protein source, the high prevalence of E. coli, antibiotic resistance, and virulence factors suggests that these could pose public health risks. These findings indicate that strict hygiene measures may be needed in fish processing and consumption.

title: Genomic insights into the probiotic safety, butyrate production, and type-II L-Asparaginase of Bacillus altitudinis AHK-Y5
abstract: Bacillus altitudinis is a resilient, spore-forming, Gram-positive bacterium. It thrives in soil, water, air, plant roots, and the human gut. It is a potential candidate for various industrial, biomedical, and biotechnological applications. This study analyzes an airborne B. altitudinis strain, AHK-Y5 for genome-based safety assessment (GBSA), and production and in silico analysis of L-asparaginase. The genome has 3.7 million base pairs and 3,822 genes. It lacks virulence and drug resistance genes and does not hold pathogenicity. It reveals genes that digest carbohydrates, produce short-chain fatty acids, vitamins, bacteriocins, and aid colonization. Metabolic analysis links B. altitudinis AHK-Y5 to probiotic strains like Bacillus subtilis 168 and Bacillus clausii KSM-K16. B. altitudinis AHK-Y5 produces a type-II L-asparaginase (BaltASNase) which is encoded by the ansZ gene and has a Kof 7.47 µM and a Vof 30.30 µM/min, making it a great fit for medical and industrial uses. In silico analysis predicted an extended half-life, high solubility, low hydrophobicity, favorable immunogenicity despite low antigenic potency, and stability against serine proteases such as thrombin and factor Xa. Molecular docking shows it binds best to L-asparagine with a high energy of -4.92 Kcal/mol and a 1.08 Å RMSD compared to D-asparagine, bis-acrylamide and L-lysine. In conclusion, Bacillus altitudinis AHK-Y5 lacks genes for toxins, virulence, or transmissible antibiotic resistance. Genomic analysis identified the strain as a type-II L-asparaginase producer and revealed probiotic potential through genes linked to acid and bile tolerance, adhesion, and vitamin biosynthesis; however, experimental validation is required.

title: Oral Staphylococcus carriage in healthy adults: prevalence, antimicrobial resistance, temporal patterns, and oral-nasal comparisons
abstract: The oral cavity is increasingly recognized as a reservoir of Staphylococcus species, yet knowledge gaps remain regarding species diversity, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), overlap with nasal carriage, and colonization persistence. Therefore, this study characterized oral and nasal Staphylococcus colonization in healthy young adults and explored the oral cavity as a potential niche for AMR surveillance. Staphylococcus spp. from oral and nasal samples of 101 dentistry students were isolated and identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS). Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed using EUCAST/CLSI guidelines. Longitudinal oral samples from a subgroup were analysed by Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy-Attenuated Total Reflectance (FTIR-ATR) to explore strain persistence and turnover. Staphylococcus colonization was highly prevalent (oral: 91%; nasal: 95%), with 86% concurrent oro-nasal colonization. Staphylococcus epidermidis predominated in both niches. Resistance to ≥ 1 antimicrobial was detected in 80% of coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) and 73% of oral Staphylococcus aureus carriers. Multidrug-resistant phenotypes were found in 10% of CoNS carriers. Although multidrug-resistant and methicillin-resistant S. aureus was not detected, oral S. aureus frequently showed resistance to commonly prescribed dental antibiotics (amoxicillin, erythromycin, and clindamycin). Resistance frequencies were comparable between niches. Oral species-specific colonization dynamics suggested temporal turnover among Staphylococcus warneri and persistence-like clustering for S. aureus in some participants. Oral cavity harbours diverse, frequently antimicrobial-resistant Staphylococcus populations at rates comparable to the nasal cavity. These findings support the oral cavity as a complementary niche for Staphylococcus carriage, highlighting its relevance for future AMR-surveillance strategies in dentistry and human health.

title: Development of vaccines against hospital-causing and antibiotic-resistant pathogens
abstract: The increasing prevalence of healthcare-associated infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria highlights the urgent need for alternative preventive strategies. Recombinant protein-based vaccines represent a promising approach to prevent infections caused by clinically important bacterial pathogens. This study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity of 19 recombinant protein vaccine candidates targeting Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli. Target antigens were identified, codon-optimized, and cloned into the pET28a(+) expression vector. Recombinant plasmids were transformed into E. coli TOP10 for amplification and E. coli BL21 for protein expression. A total of 147 male BALB/c mice were immunized with the recombinant protein candidates. Humoral immune responses were assessed by measuring antigen-specific serum IgG levels on days 7, 21, and 35 using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). In addition, the effects of immunization on the expression of bacterial virulence-associated genes during experimental bacteraemia were evaluated using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Codon optimization successfully increased the Codon Adaptation Index (CAI) values to above 0.80. Immunization resulted in significant reductions in the expression of Q9HY88 and PA2837 in P. aeruginosa, bamA in E. coli, and cusC and ompN in K. pneumoniae. ELISA results demonstrated a progressive increase in antigen-specific IgG levels, with peak responses observed on days 21 and 35. These preliminary findings indicate that the evaluated recombinant protein candidates are immunogenic and may influence the expression of selected bacterial virulence-associated genes in vivo. These results support further investigation of these antigens as potential components of recombinant protein-based vaccine strategies against infections caused by MDR bacterial pathogens.

title: Bacterial profile, antimicrobial resistance, and predictors of mortality in necrotizing fasciitis: a multicentre prospective study in Uganda
abstract: Necrotizing fasciitis carries a high mortality burden in low-resource settings, yet data from Uganda are scarce. This study aimed to describe the bacterial profile, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, and predictors of mortality among patients with necrotizing fasciitis in Uganda. A prospective hospital-based study was conducted among patients with surgically confirmed necrotizing fasciitis at Mubende, Hoima, and Fort Portal Regional Referral Hospitals between April and August 2025. Wound swabs and tissue samples were cultured for bacterial identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and patients were followed until discharge or death. Modified Poisson regression was used to identify independent predictors of mortality. Among 64 patients (56.3% male), median age group was 13-18 years, most had Type I polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis (60.9%), while Type II monomicrobial infections accounted for 29.7%. Streptococcus spp. (24.6%) and Staphylococcus spp. (20.2%) were the most common isolates. While Streptococcus spp. remained highly susceptible to Ceftriaxone (92.9%) and Clindamycin (96.4%), Staphylococcus spp. resistance to Ampicillin (73.9%), though retained sensitivity to Vancomycin (87.0%); Escherichia coli (18.4%) and Klebsiella spp. (14.9%) exhibited multi-drug resistance but remained largely susceptible to carbapenems (Imipenem/Meropenem, 95-100%) and Ciprofloxacin (> 90%). Anaerobes: Bacteroides and Clostridium spp were reported. Diabetes mellitus, prior use of herbal medicine, undernutrition, and anaerobic bacterial infection (all p < 0.05) despite anaerobes showing high sensitivity to Metronidazole (75-100%). Necrotizing fasciitis carries high mortality in Uganda, with anaerobic infection, diabetes, herbal medicine use, and undernutrition as key predictors; empiric therapy in low-resource settings should include anaerobic coverage with metronidazole or clindamycin.

title: Providencia spp. as emerging clinical pathogens in the era of antimicrobial resistance: From opportunism to global threat: A review
abstract: Providencia species are increasingly recognized as clinically important opportunistic pathogens, particularly in healthcare settings where the presence of vulnerable patients, prolonged hospital stays, invasive devices, and exposure to antibiotics contribute to their persistence and spread. Although Providencia spp. are historically viewed as relatively rare causes of human infection, some species such as Providencia stuartii and Providencia rettgeri have emerged as significant pathogens of urinary tract, bloodstream, respiratory, and other healthcare-associated infections. Recent studies have greatly expanded our understanding of this genus, revealing previously unknown species diversity, improved taxonomy, and identified the emergence of internationally disseminated high-risk lineages. Of particular concern is the growing burden of antimicrobial resistance. Providencia combines an intrinsically limited susceptibility profile with an increasing ability to acquire extended-spectrum β-lactamases, carbapenemases, aminoglycoside resistance determinants, quinolone resistance mechanisms, and other resistance genes. Carbapenem resistance, particularly that mediated by NDM-type metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs), has become a major clinical threat. Of great concern, the emergence of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains was reported in Providencia and it is increasingly limiting treatment options. This review summarizes the latest developments in taxonomy, epidemiology, healthcare-associated transmission, mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance, and therapeutic challenges for Providencia species, with emphasis on necessity of future research to strengthen genomic surveillance and antimicrobial resistance monitoring, promote the prudent use of antimicrobials, implement infection prevention measures, and conduct future therapeutic studies to limit further spread and improve the management of these emerging pathogens.

title: Beyond pathogen-intrinsic resistance: the host context in AMR evolution
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is traditionally viewed as a pathogen-intrinsic, genetically encoded trait. However, growing evidence indicates that antimicrobial susceptibility is dynamically shaped by the host context during an infection. Gradients in oxygen, nutrients, pH, immune effectors, spatial structure, and polymicrobial interactions generate a highly dynamic microenvironment that can profoundly influence microbial physiology and drug response. Within each of these gradient niches, pathogens can frequently occupy metabolic states that alter their kill kinetics, promote tolerance, and enable persistence even without intrinsic genetic elements. Experimental models of infection further demonstrate that antimicrobial efficacy depends not only on drug potency and microbial genotype, but also on host-imposed constraints. In this review, we highlight a systems-level framework in which AMR emerges from dynamic interactions between the pathogen, host microenvironment, and antimicrobial exposure. Such a framework takes into account tolerance, persistence, and resistance along a physiological continuum shaped by a dynamic host-pathogen-drug interaction. Therefore, recognizing AMR as an emergent property of a dynamic interplay between host-pathogen and drug exposure challenges reliance on standardizedsusceptibility testing and underscores the need for physiologically relevant infection models. By incorporating host context into experimental design and therapeutic strategy, this framework offers a more mechanistic understanding of antimicrobial susceptibility and resistance evolution, and suggests new avenues to be explored for therapeutic development and future research.

title: Phage display identification of MCR-1-targeting nanobodies to restore colistin susceptibility
abstract: The spread of antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacilli, particularly withinand non-fermentative gram-negative bacilli, poses a serious and escalating threat to global public health. Colistin, a cationic antimicrobial peptide, remains a last-line treatment for infections caused by multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria. However, the global dissemination of the plasmid-encoded colistin resistance gene mobilized colistin resistance-1 () has contributed to increasing cases of colistin resistance and threatens global health. Nanobodies offer advantages, including high affinity, stability, and small size. Here, we isolated anti-MCR-1.1 nanobodies from a phage-display library and evaluated their potential to restore colistin efficacy. The periplasmic catalytic domain of MCR-1.1 was purified by affinity chromatography and used to immunize alpacas, resulting in the construction of a phage-displayed nanobody library against MCR-1.1 with a size of 5.8 × 10⁸ CFU. After biopanning, several anti-MCR-1.1 nanobodies specific for the periplasmic catalytic domain of MCR-1.1 were successfully isolated. Among them, high-affinity nanobodies Nb7, Nb12, Nb24, and Nb30 were selected, with Nb30 demonstrating promising activity. Following engineering, the Nb30-1 variant was generated and shown to exhibit enhanced efficacy. In combination with colistin, Nb30-1 effectively inhibited the growth of colistin-resistant, MCR-1.1-expressing laboratoryBL21(DE3), as determined by the growth dynamics curve. Molecular docking analysis revealed the binding interactions between Nb30/Nb30-1 and the MCR-1.1 protein, and affinity measurements confirmed their high binding affinity for the MCR-1.1 antigen. Given the exquisite conservation of key catalytic residues and the epitope recognized by Nb30-1 across MCR-1 variants, Nb30-1 represents a promising macromolecular adjuvant strategy to overcome MCR-1-mediated resistance.IMPORTANCEThe escalating use of antibiotics has driven a global rise in antibiotic resistance, underscoring an urgent need for adjuvants that can restore the susceptibility of drug-resistant bacteria. In this study, we isolate anti-MCR-1 nanobodies from a phage-display library and evaluate their potential to restore colistin efficacy. Following engineering, the Nb30-1 variant was generated and shown to exhibit enhanced efficacy. These findings suggest that engineered anti-MCR-1 nanobodies, particularly Nb30-1, represent a promising therapeutic strategy to combat MCR-1-positive colistin-resistant bacterial infections by resensitizing bacteria to colistin.

title: Draft genome sequence of a multidrug-resistant, CTX-M-15-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae ST16 isolate from a dog in Bangladesh
abstract: We report the draft genome sequence of a multidrug-resistant,-producingsequence type 16 (ST16) isolate recovered from a dog in Chattogram, Bangladesh. The 5.4-Mb genome was assembled into 85 contigs (, 232.4 kb; GC content, 57.3%) and carries bla, bla, bla, bla, and 40 additional antimicrobial resistance genes.

title: Draft genome sequences of six Escherichia coli isolates from urinary tract infections in New Zealand
abstract: is a leading global cause of urinary tract infections and exhibits high rates of antibiotic resistance. We report the draft genome sequences of six trimethoprim-resistantisolates representing low, medium, and high resistance obtained from urine specimens of de-identified patients from Middlemore Hospital Laboratory, Auckland, New Zealand.

title: Full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences of lettuce-associated bacterial communities across soil-root compartments under antibiotic exposure
abstract: Antibiotic contamination in agricultural soils poses increasing threats to plant-associated microbiome structure and function. Here, we present a full-length 16S rRNA gene amplicon data set generated from lettuce soil-root compartments under sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim exposure. The data set provides a resource for investigating compartment-specific microbiome responses to pharmaceutical contamination in agricultural systems.

title: High Prevalence of Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative Bacteria on Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Surfaces at a Tertiary Hospital in Kampala, Uganda
abstract: About 60% of neonatal sepsis cases are hospital-acquired and are often caused by Gram-negative bacteria, with a high rate of antimicrobial resistance. Outbreaks of multidrug-resistant bacteria in neonatal units occur at rates 20 times higher in low- and middle-income countries than in high-income settings. We conducted 4 rounds (R1-4) of environmental sampling in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) in Kampala, Uganda, to inform an infection prevention and control (IPC) program tailored to a resource-limited setting. Eighty-two swabs were taken over 12 months (2021-2022) from n = 13 high-touch surfaces, n = 10 low-touch surfaces (R1-3) and n = 6 staff items (R4). Potential pathogens were identified using standard biochemical methods. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion. Hand hygiene audits were conducted throughout the study period. A collaborative working group of NICU, IPC and research staff co-developed IPC interventions. Of 146 organisms isolated, 127 (82%) were potential pathogens, predominantly Pseudomonas spp., Acinetobacter spp. and Citrobacter spp. High-touch sites such as sinks, cots and drug trolleys showed persistent contamination. Resistance to first-line antibiotics was high: gentamicin (48/91, 52%), ampicillin (25/25, 100%) and ceftazidime (30/91, 33%). After color-coded feedback, a unit-wide deep clean reduced potential pathogens by 60% from R1 (n = 63) to R2 (n = 25). However, levels rebounded in R3 (n = 32), representing a 21% increase compared with R2 (n = 25), highlighting inconsistencies in cleaning. Targeted environmental cleaning can reduce NICU contamination by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacterial pathogens. Sinks were persistent reservoirs, underscoring the need for consistent daily cleaning and staff engagement. In low- and middle-income country settings, simple, low-cost IPC measures informed by environmental surveillance may support sustainable hospital-acquired infection reduction.

title: Epidemiology, risk factors, and antimicrobial susceptibility of nasopharyngeal bacterial colonization in children: A prospective study using culture and PCR
abstract: To investigate bacterial carriage among Taiwanese children, focusing on colonization patterns, risk factors, and antibiotic susceptibility. In this prospective hospital-based study, children aged 1 month to <13 years were recruited from well-child/vaccination clinics, general pediatric outpatient clinics, and pediatric inpatient wards from March to November 2025. Nasopharyngeal specimens were analyzed using culture and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed for cultured isolates. Risk factors for carriage were evaluated. Among 346 children, carriage of Moraxella catarrhalis (59%) was most prevalent, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (35.8%), Haemophilus influenzae (23.1%), and Staphylococcus aureus (15.6%), as determined by combined culture and qPCR results. PCR increased detection and identified frequent co-colonization (42.5%). S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae carriage peaked at 1-2 years, whereas S. aureus showed a U-shaped distribution. Daycare attendance (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 7.761, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.396-17.738), recent upper respiratory tract infection (aOR = 4.704, 95% CI: 2.626-8.428), allergic diseases (aOR = 3.441, 95% CI: 1.857-6.379), and prior otitis media (aOR = 2.385, 95% CI: 1.151-4.943) were independently associated with carriage. Penicillin resistance in S. pneumoniae was low (5.3%, non-meningitis breakpoints). Ampicillin resistance was common in H. influenzae (63.8%) and M. catarrhalis (54.3%), but both remained susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanate (93.6% and 100%). Nasopharyngeal carriage in children is common, often polymicrobial, and age-dependent. PCR improves detection over culture. Local carriage surveillance may complement clinical isolate data and help monitor antimicrobial resistance trends.

title: AI-driven precision anti-infective therapy in critical care
abstract: Severe infections, including sepsis and those caused by multidrug-resistant organisms, remain a persistent and significant global critical care challenge, leading to substantial morbidity, high mortality rates, and immense healthcare resource strain. Effective management is critically dependent on addressing the complex and time-sensitive needs for rapid diagnosis, timely antimicrobial therapy, accurate prediction of pathogenic microorganisms and antimicrobial resistance, and personalized therapeutic adjustment. Traditional methods, which often rely on non-specific scores and delayed results, are frequently insufficient for these dynamic, high-stakes clinical decisions. Artificial Intelligence have thus emerged as highly promising, transformative tools. We searched five databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of science, Cochrane library, and Scopus) from inception to October 2025 for studies involving AI methods applied to patients with severe infections. Eligible study designs included randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, and case series. Data extraction focused on AI models, patient populations, outcomes, and management strategy application across five key clinical domains. A total of 78 studies met the inclusion criteria. AI models demonstrated significant utility in infection types and sepsis risk assessment, achieving high sensitivity and specificity in early detection. Substantial progress was also identified in the prediction of antimicrobial resistance and the implementation of optimal antimicrobial therapy and timing. Furthermore, AI enhanced the prediction of prognosis and mortality and provided tailored strategies for optimization for special populations. The continuous advancement and development of machine learning models have improved the accuracy of predictions. AI technologies show immense promise across the entire spectrum of severe infection management, from early risk assessment to precision antibiotic dosing and prognosis prediction. While the field is burgeoning with high-performing models, standardized clinical validation and rigorous implementation studies are essential to translate this technological potential into widespread clinical practice and improved patient outcomes.

title: Outbreak of multifactorial septicaemia in weaned piglets with parallel presence of H1N1pdm09 swine influenza virus: A case report
abstract: A disease outbreak associated with increased mortality in weaned piglets aged 7-8 weeks in an intensive production system is described. The disease was characterised by a progressive increase in morbidity and mortality over a three-week period, with the number of clinical cases rising from approximately 30 in the first week to more than 100 cases per week thereafter. The clinical course was marked by progressive weakness, dyspnoea, dehydration, and high mortality, with the most severely affected individuals being those in poor body condition. Gross pathological examination revealed fibrinous polyserositis with variable involvement of the peritoneum, pleura, pericardium and joints, accompanied by fibrinous pneumonia consistent with systemic bacterial infection. Molecular diagnostics confirmed the presence of swine influenza virus (SIV, H1N1pdm09, pandemic 2009 lineage) and Glaesserella parasuis in pooled tissue samples, whereas porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) was not detected. Bacteriological examination identified multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium. These findings indicate a complex multifactorial aetiopathogenesis within the porcine respiratory disease complex (PRDC), characterised by the parallel presence of H1N1pdm09 SIV and multiple bacterial pathogens associated with systemic disease and septicaemia.

title: Population structure, pathogenic potential, and antimicrobial resistance of Streptococcus suis serotype 16
abstract: Streptococcus suis is an important swine pathogen with numerous serotypes, and different serotypes vary considerably in population structure, pathogenicity, and antimicrobial resistance. Serotype 16 is one of the serotypes reported to infect humans, yet its population structure, pathogenic potential, and resistance characteristics remain poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 303 serotype 16 strains from 13 countries and found high genetic diversity, clear geographical clustering, and three distinct phylogenetic groups. Notably, some serotype 16 strains exhibited high virulence in zebrafish and mouse models and strong cytotoxicity toward human lung adenocarcinoma and brain microvascular endothelial cells. Among the 107 isolates tested phenotypically, 99.07% were multidrug resistant and 39.25% were resistant to penicillin. Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) and prophages were identified as major vehicles associated with the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes. Remarkably, the vast majority of ICE‑carrying genomes (88.00%, 44/50) clustered within group 2-2, indicating that this group may have greater potential for ICE-mediated horizontal dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes. In addition, ICEs from these strains showed high similarity to elements identified in a highly pathogenic human-derived S. suis strain and Streptococcus agalactiae, indicating potential cross-species genetic exchange. Together, these findings reveal substantial genetic diversity, pathogenic potential, and widespread multidrug resistance in S. suis serotype 16, underscoring the need for continued surveillance.

title: EaRly impAct theraPy with ceftazidime-avibactam via rapID diagnostics versus standard of care antibiotics and diagnostics in patients with bloodstream infection, hospital-acquired pneumonia or ventilator-associated pneumonia due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa or carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (RAPID): protocol for a randomised controlled trial
abstract: Rapid microbiological diagnostics have the potential for improving patient outcomes through timely and targeted antibiotic therapy and reduced selective pressure for multidrug resistant infections. However, the benefit of rapid diagnostics in terms of patient outcomes has yet to be shown in a randomised trial. This is a phase 4, multinational, open label, randomised superiority trial. PotentiBIOFIRE® FILMARRAY® Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) Panelal participants are hospitalised patients whose blood or respiratory samples yieldor multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales. Participants with ventilator-associated pneumonia should meet the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Healthcare Safety Network criteria. Consented participants are randomised into two groups. Participants in the intervention arm will have their blood or respiratory samples undergo the BIOFIRE® FILMARRAY® Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) Panel or the BIOFIRE® FILMARRAY® Pneumonia (PN) Panel, BIOFIRE® FILMARRAY® Pneumonia plus (PNplus) Panel respectively along with standard of care diagnostics. Following which, these patients will receive early targeted antibiotic therapy according to locally adapted antibiotic stewardship guidelines. Ceftazidime-avibactam is administered for infections caused byor carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales. Participants in the control arm will receive standard of care diagnostics and antibiotics. The primary endpoint is a composite measure of all-cause mortality and absence of improvement in sequential organ failure assessment score at Day 14 post index culture. Secondary endpoints include clinical response, duration of hospitalisation, antibiotic usage, development of antibiotic resistance and functional outcomes. A total of 1526 participants are required to achieve 80% power, assuming 30% treatment failure in the control arm, reducing to 24% in the intervention arm and 5% cross-over or loss to follow-up from each arm. Statistical analysis will be performed based on both intention-to-treat and per-protocol study populations. The study has received approval from the Domain Specific Review Board within the National Healthcare Group in Singapore (reference 2024-4014) and from the respective local ethics committee at each study site. The National University of Singapore Institutional Review Board granted an exemption from review (NUS-IRB-2023-265). Study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, presentations at national and international scientific conferences, and communication with patients, healthcare professionals, policymakers and relevant stakeholders. title: High rates of carbapenem resistance and inappropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy in Acinetobacter bloodstream infection in Vietnam: A single-centre retrospective study
abstract: We described the antimicrobial resistance profile of Acinetobacter spp. isolated from blood cultures and assessed the appropriateness of empirical antimicrobial therapy in patients with Acinetobacter bloodstream infection (BSI) in Vietnam. This was a retrospective cohort study of all culture-confirmed Acinetobacter BSI episodes at Hanoi Medical University Hospital (HMUH) between January 2021 and December 2024. Empirical treatment was defined as any systemic antimicrobial initiated before the blood culture result was available and administered for at least 48 hours. It was classified as appropriate when the isolate was susceptible to at least one administered antimicrobial, and as inappropriate when the isolate was intermediate or resistant to all administered antimicrobials. Fifty-six Acinetobacter BSI episodes were included, of which 51 (91.1%) were caused by the Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii (ACB) complex and 5 (8.9%) by non-ACB species. Carbapenem resistance was present in 39/56 isolates (69.6%). Overall in-hospital mortality proportion was 21/56 (37.5%). Empirical antimicrobial treatment was appropriate in only 6/56 (10.7%) episodes, inappropriate or absent in 37/56 (66.1%), and indeterminate in 13/56 (23.2%). Appropriate empirical therapy was less frequent in carbapenem-resistant than in non- carbapenem-resistant episodes (1/39, 2.6% versus 5/17, 29.4%; p = 0.008). Among ACB complex episodes, in-hospital mortality proportion was 16/35 (45.7%) in the inappropriate group versus 1/5 (20.0%) in the appropriate group. Inappropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy was common in Acinetobacter BSI due to the high prevalence of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter. These findings highlight the urgency of developing risk-stratified empirical treatment guidance for Acinetobacter BSI in Vietnam.

title: How to navigate infectious disease mathematical models: a guide for clinicians
abstract: Infectious diseases are characterised by transmission between hosts, creating population dynamics that distinguish them from non-communicable diseases. Because these dynamics are difficult to measure empirically, mathematical models are used to capture them and evaluate interventions, including scenarios that would be impractical or impossible to study directly. Clinicians increasingly encounter such modelling studies in decisions about clinical practice and public health, and need to be able to understand and interpret them. To introduce fundamental concepts in infectious disease transmission modelling and provide practical guidance for clinicians to understand modelling studies and critically interpret their findings in clinical and public health contexts. This narrative review draws on peer-reviewed literature on infectious disease transmission modelling, using bacterial infections and interventions to reduce antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as illustrative examples. We propose a practical checklist to support the interpretation of infectious disease modelling studies. The checklist guides clinicians in understanding which clinical or public health question a model addresses, which assumptions and parameters shape the model, how uncertain the results are, whether the model and its results are valid, and what the results mean for clinical and public health. As with empirical studies, understanding how an infectious disease modelling study was conducted is essential for critically interpreting findings before applying them to practice. The proposed checklist offers clinicians a practical framework to do so.

title: Habitat disturbance associated with habitat-use strategies is linked to divergence in gut opportunistic pathogen communities and resistomes of overwintering waterbirds
abstract: Within the One Health framework, wild animals, particularly migratory waterbirds, are considered potential carriers of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and opportunistic pathogens. However, how habitat-use strategies shape gut opportunistic pathogen communities and the resistome remains unclear. We selected 6 overwintering waterbird species using high- or low-disturbance habitat-use strategies and, based on metagenomic analyses, examined the distribution and differences of ARGs and opportunistic pathogens. We identified 991 ARG subtypes belonging to 27 ARG types across the 6 waterbird species, dominated by the multidrug, bacitracin, and polymyxin classes, with higher abundances of ARGs among high-disturbance group. The high-risk ARG composition differed, and some high-risk ARGs had higher relative abundances in Black-necked Crane, whereas bacA dominated all samples. Additionally, 85 opportunistic pathogen species were detected. Pseudomonas fluorescens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia were significantly enriched in the high-disturbance group, whereas Acinetobacter lwoffii exhibited higher abundances in the low-disturbance group, both groups may therefore pose potential health risks. Metagenomic binning revealed more MAGs carrying both ARGs and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) in the high-disturbance group, predominantly assigned to Pseudomonas_E. Furthermore, agriculture soil showed a greater potential contribution to the ARG profiles of high-disturbance-group waterbirds than to those of low-disturbance-group waterbirds (26.21% vs. 21.17%). These findings suggest that habitat disturbance is associated with variations in gut opportunistic pathogen communities and resistome composition in overwintering waterbirds, potentially entailing certain risks. They provide important insights into the ecological security and public health risks associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

title: Population dynamics and antimicrobial resistance of S. pneumoniae in China based on Genomic surveillance
abstract: Widespread pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) usage has reshaped the Streptococcus pneumoniae population and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) globally. However, under the unique ecological setting of critically low PCV coverage and intensive antimicrobial consumption in China, the genomic epidemiological characteristics of prevalent pneumococcal strains remain largely unclear. To characterize circulating S. pneumoniae lineages in China, 2841 isolates collected across 29 provinces between 2008 and 2025 were compared against global genomes. Pipelines were used for serotyping, Global Pneumococcal Sequence Cluster (GPSC) assignment, and PCV coverage estimation. AMR was predicted via resistance gene identification and random forest modeling, while phylogenetic and recombination analyses elucidated the evolutionary dynamics of GPSC12 and GPSC3 lineages. From 2008 to 2025, the Chinese S. pneumoniae population has been dominated by the multidrug-resistant GPSC1, which drives penicillin non-susceptibility despite its recent temporal decline. This population imposes a severe AMR burden, with 98.87% of isolates resistant to at least one class; specifically, resistance rates were 97.18% for macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B (MLSb), 97.15% for tetracycline, and 79.23% for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Estimated coverage for PCV13, PCV15, and PCV20 was 72.69%, 73.39%, and 78.35%, respectively. Notably, the expansion of the serotype 3 lineages GPSC12 and GPSC3 signals a shift in population dynamics: GPSC12 maintains its serotype 3 phenotype via a highly conserved cps locus, whereas GPSC3 acquired this phenotype through an ancestral capsular switch and rapid clonal dissemination. Our findings demonstrate that China exhibits a distinctly different pneumococcal genomic landscape compared to countries with routine PCV programs. This unique structure is defined by an extreme, GPSC1-driven multidrug resistance burden and active temporal shifts, including the progressive expansion of divergent serotype 3 lineages. Despite these epidemiological and antimicrobial resistance challenges, existing PCVs retain substantial potential serotype coverage against the circulating pneumococcal population in China. These findings highlight the urgent need for sustained longitudinal genomic surveillance and underscore the substantial potential of PCV in optimizing precision disease control.

title: Exploring the integration of Ayurveda in aquaculture: A scoping review
abstract: Aquaculture is a rapidly growing food-producing sector, but its sustainability is challenged by infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance, environmental degradation, poor water quality, and dependence on antibiotics and synthetic chemicals. This scoping review mapped the available evidence on Ayurveda-associated medicinal plants and botanical interventions used in aquaculture for improving growth performance, feed conversion, innate immunity, disease resistance, gut health, stress tolerance, and water quality. The review was conducted following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Literature published between January 2010 and March 2026 was searched in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. A total of 61 studies met the inclusion criteria. Frequently investigated botanicals included Withania somnifera, Tinospora cordifolia, Curcuma longa, Azadirachta indica, Ocimum tenuiflorum, Allium sativum, Zingiber officinale, Aloe vera, Andrographis paniculata, Phyllanthus spp., and Moringa oleifera. Reported benefits included improved growth performance, feed conversion, digestive enzyme activity, lysozyme and complement activity, antioxidant status, survival, gut microbiota modulation, and reduced susceptibility to bacterial, viral, and parasitic infections. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous, with variations in species, plant preparations, doses, duration, and outcome measures. No direct aquaculture studies evaluating classical Ayurvedic polyherbal formulations were identified; therefore, such formulations are discussed only as hypothesis-generating candidates for future research. Ayurveda-associated medicinal plants may offer sustainable phytogenic options for aquaculture, but practical application requires standardization, phytochemical characterization, safety evaluation, dose optimization, commercial-scale field trials, economic assessment, and supportive regulatory frameworks.

title: Rapid detection of beta-lactamase genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli from positive blood cultures using nanopore sequencing
abstract: andare major Enterobacterales pathogens that commonly harbor beta-lactamase enzymes conferring antimicrobial resistance. Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) is time-consuming and may delay appropriate antibiotic treatment, whereas nanopore sequencing enables real-time genetic analysis and may support rapid antimicrobial resistance detection at the point of care. This study evaluated the performance of nanopore sequencing for detecting ceftriaxone and carbapenem resistance in positive blood cultures containingor. In this cross-sectional descriptive study, positive blood culture samples yieldingorwere analyzed. Bacterial DNA was extracted and sequenced in its native form using the PromethION nanopore platform to detect antimicrobial resistance genes, and sequencing-based predictions were compared with routine blood culture results and standard AST. A total of 62and 96samples met the inclusion criteria for DNA extraction and sequencing. Simulated real-time analysis showed that the optimal condition for detecting third-generation cephalosporin and carbapenem resistance genes was approximately 1 h of sequencing, using a sequence divergence threshold of <0.001 against the antimicrobial resistance gene database. For third-generation cephalosporin resistance, sensitivity was 87.0% (95% CI: 79.5%-94.5%) and specificity was 77.8% (95% CI: 68.7%-86.8%); for carbapenem resistance, sensitivity was 77.8% (95% CI: 58.6%-97.0%) and specificity was 96.4% (95% CI: 93.4%-99.5%). Overall, nanopore sequencing is feasible for rapid detection of ceftriaxone and carbapenem resistance directly from positive blood cultures, although further optimization is needed to improve accuracy.IMPORTANCEBloodstream infections can progress rapidly and require timely selection of effective antimicrobial therapy. However, conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing typically requires 2-3 days, which may delay optimal treatment. In this study, nanopore sequencing detected key antimicrobial resistance genes inanddirectly from positive blood cultures after approximately 1 h of sequencing. This approach could support earlier prediction of antibiotic resistance and help guide more timely treatment decisions for patients with serious infections. The study also identified important limitations, including incorrect predictions for ceftriaxone and carbapenem resistance in some samples. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of rapid DNA sequencing to improve the management of bloodstream infections, while emphasizing that further improvement in predictive accuracy is needed before routine implementation in clinical laboratories.

title: Economic value of gonorrhea resistance testing in the United States: A multi-perspective modeling study
abstract: Rising antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens the effectiveness of existing therapies. Ceftriaxone is the only recommended first-line (empiric) treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea in the United States. Ciprofloxacin is no longer recommended for empiric use because of widespread resistance, but it is inexpensive, taken orally, and effective against susceptible infections, which a resistance test can identify. In the context of rising resistance, resistance-guided treatment (RGT) may reduce treatment failures, complications, and inappropriate use of last-line agents while slowing resistance emergence and preserving the efficacy of new and existing drugs. Understanding where RGT provides economic value-across near-term cost savings, delayed resistance emergence, and avoided antibiotic development costs-can illuminate the broader case for investing in resistance testing and help guide pricing and reimbursement decisions. We developed an individual-level stochastic simulation model of gonorrhea diagnosis and treatment in the United States, incorporating infection prevalence, symptom status, diagnostic accuracy, resistance profiles, treatment pathways, and partner management (costs in 2025 US dollars[USD]). We evaluated three resistance testing strategies, ciprofloxacin-only, ciprofloxacin + ceftriaxone, and triple-target (including a novel drug A), across a wide range of resistance scenarios. We quantified economic value across three dimensions: (1) per-episode direct medical cost savings, (2) system-level costs attributable to ceftriaxone resistance emergence among men who have sex with men (MSM), and (3) avoided costs of new antibiotic development, estimating the maximum per-test price at which RGT remains cost-neutral. Per-episode cost-neutrality thresholds ranged from near $0 when ceftriaxone resistance was absent to up to $48 per test at 15% prevalence of ceftriaxone resistance (proportion of infections resistant to ceftriaxone). At a prevalence of 50% ciprofloxacin resistance and 5% ceftriaxone resistance, the population-weighted threshold was $7 (95% uncertainty interval [UI] ($3, $11) for a ciprofloxacin-only test and $13 (95% UI [$8-$19]) for a triple-target test. Among MSM, incorporating system-level resistance emergence costs and avoided antibiotic development costs increased the total per-test value to $31 to $114 for a single-target test and $73 to $106 for a triple-target test, depending on whether prescribing practices shift when ceftriaxone resistance reaches 5%. The main limitations are that the model assumes resistance results are available at the same clinical visit to guide initial treatment, does not represent onward transmission or co-resistance between antibiotics, and could estimate longer-term value only for MSM. Resistance-guided therapy offers economic benefits across multiple dimensions even at relatively high diagnostic prices, supporting investment in gonorrhea resistance testing to improve partner outcomes, delay resistance emergence, and enhance the long-term cost-efficiency of gonorrhea management.

title: Doxycycline Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Among HIV and PrEP Providers in Two NYC Academic Medical Centers: A Cross-Sectional Pilot Survey
abstract: Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) reduces sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among vulnerable populations. Effective implementation depends on willingness to prescribe, yet data on provider knowledge, attitudes, and practices in New York City (NYC) remain limited. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of providers at two NYC academic medical centers between May-September 2025. Eligibility required prescribing antiretroviral therapy or PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) to ≥ 5 patients in the prior year. The online questionnaire adapted from a PrEP acceptability instrument measured provider doxy-PEP knowledge, attitudes, prescribing practices, and perceived barriers. Knowledge scores were summed from correct responses; attitudes on a 4-point Likert scale were transformed to reflect positive views and summed. Median total scores were compared between primary care (non-specialists) and Infectious Disease/HIV (specialists) providers using one-sided Mann-Whitney U-tests to assess whether non-specialists had lower knowledge and attitude scores. Prescribing practices were compared with Fisher's exact test. Thirty-eight eligible providers completed the survey (28 specialists, 10 non-specialists); 97% prescribed doxy-PEP previously. Specialists managed significantly larger HIV/PrEP patient panels (p<0.01). Non-specialists demonstrated lower objective doxy-PEP knowledge than specialists (median composite score 57% vs 86%, p < 0.01), particularly regarding efficacy and dosing. Doxy-PEP attitudes were favorable in both groups (median composite score 3.3 vs 3.4, max 4, p = 0.05). Concerns about antimicrobial resistance (49%) and side effects (30%) were the most reported prescribing barriers. Non-specialists endorsed favorable doxy-PEP attitudes but had lower objective knowledge. Barriers including resistance and adverse effects highlight opportunities for targeted education to improve doxy-PEP knowledge and prescribing confidence among generalist providers.

title: Modulating Growth Conditions and Microenvironment to Boost Antimicrobial Efficacy of Probiotics Against Pathogens
abstract: The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections highlights the need for alternative strategies to control pathogenic microorganisms. Probiotics have emerged as promising candidates due to their ability to inhibit pathogen growth. However, their potential ways of application in human medicine remain insufficiently understood. Here we investigate the antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity of selected probiotic strains, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Fibro 1 and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus Fibro 2, against clinically relevant pathogens, with the aim of generating insights to support the design of improved probiotic-based systems for wound infection treatment. Probiotics were investigated for their growth, lactic acid production, and biofilm formation in different media. A range of in vitro antimicrobial activity assays were employed, including growth inhibition and antibiofilm assays. In addition to free probiotics, probiotics incorporated into electrospun fiber mats via microchip electrospinning were investigated in in vitro biofilm models. Probiotics exhibit strain- and condition-dependent inhibitory effects, influencing both planktonic growth and biofilm development of pathogens, while metabolic analysis showed marked medium-dependent glucose utilization and lactate production. Probiotics incorporated into fiber mats retain measurable metabolic activity after encapsulation and preserve their antibiofilm activity. Overall, this study provides a deeper understanding of probiotic effects on pathogens and identifies key factors influencing antimicrobial efficacy. These findings support the rational design of enhanced probiotic-based formulations for applications in infection control and wound care.

title: Carbon Source Diversity Shapes DOM Chemodiversity and Antibiotic Resistome in Earthworm Casts
abstract: The earthworm gut acts as a hotspot for reprocessing ingested organic matter, thereby altering carbon availability. These changes reshape microbial communities and competitive interactions, potentially affecting the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in the gut. Beyond substrate amount, substrate diversity shapes these processes, yet its role remains unknown. We established microcosm experiments with a substrate-diversity gradient, combining FT-ICR MS and metagenomics to investigate dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry, microbial traits and ARGs in earthworm guts. Higher substrate diversity enriched carbon-centered metabolic genes and increased gut DOM availability, possibly through the proliferation of polysaccharide-degrading microorganisms with larger genomes. However, higher carbon availability may have increased microbial nutrient demand, accompanied by reductions in CHON-containing compounds and stronger microbial competition. ARG enrichment was associated with greater potential for microbial competition, as indicated by stronger negative microbial interactions and higher competition indices derived from genome scale metabolic models. In vitro monoculture of gut-derived pathogenic Klebsiella pneumoniae showed that substrate diversity enriched multidrug- and β-lactam-resistance genes and reshaped the resistome. Collectively, these findings suggest that increased substrate diversity modifies earthworm-driven carbon reprocessing, may reshape microbial resource competition and promote ARG enrichment, providing insights into the linkage between organic matter processing and resistome in soil fauna.

title: Millisecond Blebs Precede Nanometer Pores in Disrupting Microbial Membranes
abstract: Pore formation is a fundamental process for all forms of life. In the wake of antimicrobial resistance, drug-induced poration in microbial membranes attracts increasing interest. It is postulated that antimicrobial molecules bind to the membranes and insert into them, forming nanometer pores causing membrane disruption. Existing evidence indicates that pore formation completes within minutes but is energetically unfavorable, suggesting that there should be a transition state preceding it. Herein, we reveal such a state. Exemplified in a cecropin family of antimicrobial peptides we demonstrate that membrane blebbing occurs within milliseconds of introducing antimicrobials into membranes and manifests in the formation and rupture of elongated membrane blebs - causing membrane disruption under the first second of treatment.

title: Phage-Host Dynamics in Food Systems: Rethinking the "Lytic" and "Temperate" Paradigm
abstract: Phage-host dynamics are central to food systems because bacteriophages can threaten microbial stability while serving as tools for microbial control. In fermentations, phages compromise starter culture performance and product consistency, whereas in foods, animal production, and processing environments they are increasingly used as biocontrol agents against foodborne pathogens. Temperate phages may also influence virulence, tolerance, competition, and horizontal gene transfer, including antimicrobial resistance gene mobilization, placing phage ecology within a One Health framework. These roles have traditionally been interpreted through a binary model in which virulent phages lyse and temperate phages persist. However, reports of pseudolysogeny, carrier state, and delayed lysis have long suggested that this distinction is incomplete. Recent large-scale studies showing that virulent phages can persist through colony purification and bacterial genome assembly workflows provide the central motivation for this review. These findings suggest that long-term non-lysogenic association may be more widespread than appreciated and challenge the assumption that "lytic" phages necessarily cause immediate host elimination. In food systems, this has implications for fermentation reliability, biocontrol, surveillance, and One Health interpretation. We argue that food systems are informative settings for reassessing phage lifestyle categories, and that "lytic" should be understood as infection potential rather than guaranteed ecological outcome.

title: Engineering antimicrobial peptides through the design-build-test-learn framework
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the need for alternative anti-infective strategies. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer diverse mechanisms of action, but their translation remains constrained by poor physiological stability, host toxicity, and manufacturing costs. This review examines AMP development within a design-build-test-learn (DBTL) framework that connects computational discovery, peptide production, experimental evaluation, and iterative optimization. Proteome mining and generative artificial intelligence expand the accessible sequence space, while solid-phase synthesis, engineered microbial hosts, and cell-free systems convert selected sequences into testable molecules. Chemical modification and formulation provide complementary routes to improve stability and delivery. Standardized screening and in vivo studies then establish the evidence needed to prioritize candidates and inform subsequent design and production decisions. Throughout this cycle, activity must be optimized together with toxicity, stability, manufacturability, and delivery rather than treated as the sole measure of success. This review discusses applications in medicine, agriculture, food preservation, and biotechnology, and identifies remaining limitations in data quality, assay comparability, scale-up, and translational support. The DBTL framework provides a basis for coordinating these activities, although its practical value depends on experimentally validated feedback and application-specific development criteria.

title: Perinatal influences on the gut resistome and bacteriome in South African infants from birth to 6 months of life: insights from a shotgun metagenomics study
abstract: Antibiotic resistance (AR) is a major global health threat, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where neonatal infections remain a leading cause of death, compounded by limited surveillance and uncontrolled antibiotic use. The neonatal gut is a reservoir for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet LMIC data remain scarce. Using shotgun metagenomics, we investigated gut resistome and bacteriome dynamics in infants during their first 6 months of life. Analysis of 68 longitudinal fecal samples from 17 infants revealed 211 ARGs across 7 antibiotic classes. Beta-lactam genes (blaTEM-1 and blaTEM-10-MGH-1) dominated, accounting for 64.0% of detections and indicating substantial early-life resistance load. Non-blaTEM ARGs (e.g., cat4, tetC, aphA2) emerged between 16 and 26 weeks, reflecting ongoing microbial evolution. In this small, exploratory cohort, infant antibiotic exposure, maternal HIV with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), and cesarean delivery with maternal antibiotics were associated with higher ARG diversity; given the small, uneven subgroups, this pattern is hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive, suggesting a role for clinical and maternal factors in resistome development. The bacteriome featured diverse, resilient taxa with persistent opportunistic pathogens, including, and, which are potential ARG reservoirs. Despite sample size limitations, these findings offer valuable insight into neonatal ARG acquisition, persistence, and bacterial profiles in an LMIC setting, and point to a plausible, multifactorial interplay of maternal, clinical, and environmental influences on resistome dynamics requiring confirmation in larger cohorts. This early, pervasive resistance reservoir supports tailored antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and microbiome-informed strategies, alongside future genotypic-phenotypic surveillance.IMPORTANCEThis study provides region-specific insight into the early-life gut resistome and bacteriome of infants from a low- and middle-income setting, addressing a gap in global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance. Universal detection of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from birth highlights the establishment of a genetic resistance reservoir, even in antibiotic-naïve populations. In this small, exploratory cohort, perinatal factors, including antibiotic exposure, maternal HIV/HAART status, and delivery mode, showed patterns associated with resistome diversity and microbial succession. Although not statistically definitive, these findings suggest multifactorial drivers of early AMR emergence warranting confirmation in larger studies. Persistence of clinically important ARGs alongside opportunistic pathogens raises questions for neonatal infection management; however, these genotypic findings indicate potential rather than confirmed resistance, underscoring the need for paired phenotypic susceptibility data. This work establishes foundational longitudinal data for South Africa, informing antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and microbiome-informed interventions to mitigate AMR risk and improve infant health outcomes.
